input:
The regional delivery route under review costs $561k per year. The figure is the invoiced cost of the route as it is currently run, derived from the trip distance, the carrier rate and the trip count.

Carrier invoices for the last 12 months give 771 km per trip at $1.95 per km and 373 trips per year. These three figures together produce the annual cost: the distance per trip and the rate per kilometre between them determine the cost of a single trip, and the trip count then determines how many times that cost is incurred over the course of the year. It should be noted that empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the annual figure in effect pays for the whole of the distance that the route runs, loaded and empty together; the cost of a loaded kilometre on this route is therefore higher than the bare rate per kilometre might suggest, precisely because the empty distance is carried inside one and the same total.

The $561k figure is best understood as a record of what the route actually cost over the period in question, computed on the basis of carrier invoices. It is not a benchmark, and it carries no comparison with anything else: nothing in the figure states what the route should cost, and a saving against it could only properly be claimed from a change in one of the three quantities of which it is composed, namely fewer kilometres per trip, a lower rate per kilometre, or fewer trips per year. Each of those changes amounts to a change to the route itself or to the contract under which it is run, and the annual figure will move only when one of them is actually made. For as long as the route, the rate and the trip count stand exactly as invoiced, the annual transport cost stands at $561k, and the review of the route is, in essence, a review of those three quantities and of nothing else.
